claims.claim: In 2,293 medical inpatients aged 70 and over, 35% left hospital with worse basic daily function than 2 weeks before admission: 23% of all patients had declined before admission and not recovered by discharge, and 12% declined only during the stay; a further 20% declined before admission but recovered by discharge.
claims.supporting_passage: Two thousand two hundred ninety-three patients aged 70 and older (mean age 80, 64% women, 24% nonwhite). At the time of hospital admission, patients or their surrogates were interviewed about their independence in five ADLs (bathing, dressing, eating, transferring, and toileting) 2 weeks before admission (baseline) and at admission. Subjects were interviewed about ADL function at discharge. ... Thirty-five percent of patients declined in ADL function between baseline and discharge. This included the 23% of patients who declined between baseline and admission and failed to recover to baseline function between admission and discharge and the 12% of patients who did not decline between baseline and admission but declined between hospital admission and discharge. Twenty percent of patients declined between baseline and admission but recovered to baseline function between admission and discharge.
claims.pico_timeframe: Population: 2,293 patients aged 70 or over on the general medical service of two US hospitals (1990s). Exposure: hospital admission for medical illness. Comparator: the same person's function 2 weeks before admission. Outcome: independence in 5 basic ADLs (bathing, dressing, eating, transferring, toileting), self or surrogate report. Timeframe: 2 weeks before admission, admission, discharge.
claims.safe_wording: In a US study of 2,293 people aged 70 and over admitted to medical wards, about 1 in 3 (35 in 100) went home less able to wash, dress, eat, get in and out of bed or use the toilet than they had been two weeks before admission. Most of that loss (23 in every 100 patients) had happened before they reached hospital and had not been regained by discharge; 12 in 100 lost ability during the stay. Another 20 in 100 lost ability before admission and got it back.
claims.qualifications: Percentages are of all 2,293 patients (23 + 12 = 35). About two thirds of those who went home worse (23 of 35) had declined before admission. Function was reported by the patient or a relative, not observed. The five ADLs do not include walking, so do not say the study measured 'mobility'. Two US hospitals, published 2003, data from the 1990s (see C05-01-e).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No conflicting evidence found; the 2019 meta-analysis (C05-01-d) gives a similar pooled figure of 30% with large heterogeneity.

claims.supporting_passage: The frequency of ADL decline between baseline and discharge varied markedly with age (23%, 28%, 38%, 50%, and 63% in patients aged 70-74, 75-79, 80-84, 85-89, and > or =90, respectively, P <.001).
claims.pico_timeframe: Same cohort; crude proportions by 5-year age band; baseline (2 weeks before admission) to discharge.
claims.safe_wording: The older the person, the more often they left hospital less able than before the illness: about 1 in 4 people aged 70 to 74 (23 in 100) and nearly 2 in 3 people aged 90 and over (63 in 100).
claims.qualifications: Crude (unadjusted) proportions within each age band. Same era and setting limits as C05-01-a.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

claims.claim: After adjustment, age was not linked with decline before admission, but older age was linked with failing to recover lost function in hospital and with new losses during the stay.
claims.supporting_passage: After adjustment for potential confounders, age was not associated with ADL decline before hospitalization (odds ratio (OR) for patients aged > or =90 compared with patients aged 70-74 = 1.26, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 0.88-1.82). In contrast, age was associated with the failure to recover ADL function during hospitalization in patients who declined before admission (OR for patients aged > or =90 compared with patients aged 70-74 = 2.09, 95% CI = 1.20-3.65) and with new losses of ADL function during hospitalization in patients who did not decline before admission (OR for patients aged > or =90 compared with patients aged 70-74 = 3.43, 95% CI = 1.92-6.12).
claims.pico_timeframe: Same cohort; adjusted odds ratios, people aged 90 and over versus 70 to 74.
claims.safe_wording: The oldest patients were no more likely than younger ones to lose function before admission, but they were less likely to get it back in hospital and more likely to lose function during the stay.
claims.qualifications: Observational associations (odds ratios); do not convert to 'X times more likely'. Optional supporting claim.

claims.claim: More recent pooled evidence shows about 30% of older adults lose independence in basic daily activities after an acute hospital stay, with little change by study start year.
claims.supporting_passage: Random effects meta-analysis across included studies identified combined prevalence of HAD as 30% (95% CI 24%, 33%; P < .001). The effect of study initiation year on the prevalence rate was minimal. A large amount of heterogeneity was observed between studies, which may be due in part to nonstandardized measurement of ADL impairment or other methodological differences.
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults aged 65 and over in acute medical-surgical care; 7,375 participants across studies; ADL (Katz or Barthel) measured at 2 or more time points before or during and after hospitalisation.
claims.safe_wording: A 2019 review that pooled studies of 7,375 older adults found that about 3 in 10 lost independence in basic daily activities after an acute hospital stay, and the figure had changed little over the years the studies were done.
claims.qualifications: Studies measured function in different ways and results varied widely between studies. Definitions of the starting point differ (some before admission, some on admission).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Heterogeneity is large; the pooled figure is an average across different populations.

claims.claim: Function before admission is often not documented in hospital notes, and when it is, it misses impairment.
claims.supporting_passage: Bogardus 2001: "Subjects were 525 medical patients, aged 70 years or older, hospitalized at an academic medical center. Patient interviews determined status for 7 basic activities of daily living (BADLs) and 7 instrumental activities of daily living (IADLs). Medical records were reviewed to assess documentation of BADLs and IADLs. Most medical records contained no documentation of individual BADLs and IADLs (61% to 98% of records lacking documentation), with the exception of walking (24% of medical records lacking documentation). Impairment prevalence was lower in medical records than at interview for all BADLs and IADLs, and agreement between interview and medical record was poor (kappa < 0.40 for individual BADLs and IADLs)." ... "assuming that nondocumentation of functional status is equivalent to independence may be unwarranted." Scite Methods snippet: "The patient provided information on sociodemographics ... and preadmission BADLs and IADLs". Covinsky 2011 abstract: "Since recognition of functional status problems is an essential prerequisite to preventing and managing disability, we also describe a pragmatic approach toward functional status assessment in the hospital focused on evaluation of ADLs, mobility, and cognition."
claims.location: Bogardus 2001 Abstract (Methods, Results, Conclusions) and Methods snippet via Scite; Covinsky 2011 Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: 525 medical inpatients aged 70+, one US academic centre; interview about preadmission ADLs (reference) versus medical record documentation; cross-sectional, published 2001.
claims.safe_wording: In a US study of 525 medical patients aged 70 and over, most hospital records did not record whether the person could manage individual daily tasks before admission; walking was the exception. Where records did say something, they found less impairment than the patients themselves reported.
claims.qualifications: One centre, published 2001, paper records; electronic records may differ. Do not say 'most notes never mention function'; say individual daily tasks were usually not recorded.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No recent documentation audit was checked in this batch.

numbers.meaning: medical inpatients aged 70+
proportion of records lacking documentation of individual basic and instrumental ADLs
records lacking documentation of walking

claims.claim: Position: hospital teams should record function from about two weeks before the illness and state at discharge how far the person is from that level.
claims.supporting_passage: Covinsky 2003: "patients or their surrogates were interviewed about their independence in five ADLs ... 2 weeks before admission (baseline) and at admission." Conclusion: "Many hospitalized older people are discharged with ADL function that is worse than their baseline function." Covinsky 2011: "we also describe a pragmatic approach toward functional status assessment in the hospital focused on evaluation of ADLs, mobility, and cognition."
claims.pico_timeframe: Practice recommendation derived from cohort method and expert review; not tested in a trial.
claims.safe_wording: Present as judgement: 'We should record what the person could do two weeks before they became ill, and say at discharge how far they are from that level.' The evidence shows this baseline can be obtained at admission by asking the person or a relative, and that measuring only from admission misses loss that happened before arrival.
claims.qualifications: No trial shows that recording a pre-illness baseline improves outcomes; mark as the author's position. The discharge-letter line (two weeks before: X; now: Y) is a suggested format, not a published standard.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

claims.claim: Older women who had changed how or how often they did a mobility task, without reporting difficulty, had walking speed, balance and strength between those of women with no change and women with difficulty.
claims.supporting_passage: The Women's Health and Aging Study II, an observational study of 436 women 70-80 years of age who were among the two-thirds least disabled living in the community. ... (3) no difficulty but reported modification and/or change in frequency of task performance (a self-report measure of preclinical disability predictive of incident difficulty). ... Physical performance decreased, and disease frequency increased, in association with decreasing self-reported mobility function (in walking one-half mile and climbing 10 steps), across three self-report categories: High Function, Preclinical Disability (Task Modification but No Difficulty) and Disability (Difficulty). These findings pertained for measures of walking speed, balance, strength, and knee and hip osteoarthritis.
claims.pico_timeframe: 436 higher-functioning community-dwelling women aged 70 to 80, Baltimore; cross-sectional at the 18-month visit; self-report category versus measured walking speed, balance, strength and joint disease.
claims.safe_wording: In a Baltimore study of 436 women aged 70 to 80, those who said they had changed how or how often they walked half a mile or climbed 10 steps, but had no difficulty, were measured as slower, weaker and less steady than women with no change, though not as affected as women who reported difficulty.
claims.qualifications: Cross-sectional (one time point). Women only, the more able two thirds of the age group, one US city, data from the 1990s.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Consistent with Mänty 2007 in Finnish men and women (C05-02-d).

numbers.meaning: women aged 70 to 80, Women's Health and Aging Study II

claims.claim: In the same cohort, women without mobility difficulty who reported changing how they did a task had 3 to 4 times the odds of developing walking or stair difficulty over 18 months.
claims.supporting_passage: At baseline, 69.3% of the cohort reported no difficulty with mobility. After 18 months, 16.0 and 11.7% of this group reported incident difficulty walking 1/2 mile or climbing up 10 steps, respectively. Those reporting baseline task modification due to underlying health problems, our measure of preclinical disability, were at three- to fourfold higher odds of progressing to difficulty than were those without such modification. In multivariate logistic regression analyses, this self-report measure, task modification without difficulty, and objective measures of performance were independently and jointly predictive of incident mobility difficulty. Specifically, for incident difficulty walking 1/2 mile, self-reported task modification odds ratio (OR) = 3.67 ... for incident difficulty climbing up 10 stairs, OR for task modification = 3.84
claims.pico_timeframe: Women aged 70 to 80 without mobility difficulty at baseline (69.3% of 436); exposure: self-reported task modification without difficulty; comparator: no modification; outcome: self-reported incident difficulty walking half a mile or climbing 10 steps; 18 months; adjusted odds ratios.
claims.safe_wording: Over the next 18 months, women who had already changed how they walked or climbed stairs were more likely to develop difficulty with those tasks than women who had not changed anything, even after taking their measured walking speed into account. Overall, about 1 in 6 (16 in 100) of the women with no difficulty at the start developed difficulty walking half a mile.
claims.qualifications: Effect sizes are odds ratios; for practitioners write 'about 3 to 4 times the odds', never 'times more likely'. Absolute risks by group were not available. The 16.0% and 11.7% are for all women without mobility difficulty at baseline, not by modification group.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

claims.claim: Women who newly reported changing how or how often they walked were more likely 1.5 years later to report new walking difficulty and to have stopped walking 8 blocks outdoors; the question used was 'Have you changed the way you walk 1/2 mile, or how often you do this, due to a health or physical condition?'
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "Data are from a prospective study of 436 community-dwelling women age 70-79 years. Outcome measures include subjective and objective measures of walking ability at 3 years. ... Compared to women without, women with incident PCMD at 1.5 years after baseline were 2.7 (95%CI 1.4-7.2) times more likely to report that they no longer walk outdoors at least 8 blocks and 4.9 (1.9-13.1) times more likely to report new difficulty walking." candidates.reason: The core point is supported: changed method or frequency without difficulty marks an intermediate stage (Fried 2001, cross-sectional) that predicts later mobility difficulty (Fried 2000, odds ratios; Weiss 2012, adjusted risk ratios with wide intervals), and a Finnish study replicated it in men and women (Mänty 2007). The exact published question is available from the Weiss full text. The candidate's inference that earlier detection gives strength and balance work 'more to work with' is not supported by these sources and must go (C05-02-f). Population limits must be stated. Cite Weiss as 2012 and do not use the abstract's 2.7 figure.
candidates.revised_angle: Keep the teaching point and the single history question ('Have you changed how you do this, or how often, because of your health?'), which picks up people before they report difficulty. Evidence: women in Baltimore who had changed how they walked or climbed stairs were already slower and weaker, and were more likely to develop difficulty over the next 18 months to 3 years; a Finnish study found the same in men and women. State that the main studies were of more able women aged 70 to 79 recruited in the 1990s. Do not claim that acting at this stage prevents disability; say the researchers proposed it as a point to offer help.

candidates.reason: All essential claims are supported. Covinsky 2003 abstract confirms the percentages are of all 2,293 patients (23% + 12% = 35%; a further 20% declined and recovered) and gives the age gradient. The cohort was published in 2003 with data from the 1990s, and a 2019 meta-analysis (30%, little change by study year) shows the pattern persists. Bogardus 2001 supports poor documentation of pre-admission function. The recommended discharge-letter line is the author's judgement and must be marked as such. The ADLs measured do not include walking, so 'mobility improving' should be framed as an example of a progress note, not as what the study measured.

All essential claims are supported by the two Cochrane reviews. Hospital absolute effects were read from the Ellis 2017 summary of findings table: about 3 more in 100 alive and at home (56 to 60 in 100) and about 3 to 4 fewer in 100 in a care home (19 to 15 in 100), no difference in deaths (23 in 100) and little or no difference in dependence. Community absolute effects could not be opened, so the community row must be described in words only, with 'may' and 'low certainty' for unplanned admissions. The definition and wards-versus-teams uncertainty are supported. The position is judgement and must be marked as such.

The trial design, the 5-month relative reduction in ADL difficulty scores, the unclear IADL result, the 82% vs 43% 'made life easier' result and the population limits are supported from the full text. But absolute scores could not be found; the ADL benefit was no longer statistically clear at 12 months; and a 2025 randomised trial of CAPABLE after hospital discharge did not improve ADLs. The UK access route (GP or council) is an unverified service fact. The 'care that works' framing must carry these limits.
candidates.revised_angle: A US trial sent an occupational therapist, a nurse and a handyperson to the homes of 300 older people on low incomes to work on goals each person chose. After 5 months they reported less difficulty with washing, dressing and moving around than people who had social visits, and 8 in 10 said it made life easier (4 in 10 with social visits). Household tasks did not clearly improve, the difference faded by 12 months, and a 2025 trial after hospital discharge did not show the same benefit. The lasting point: difficulty at home comes from both the person and the house, so an assessment should look at both. Action phrased as a question (ask whether an occupational therapist can look at how you do things and at your home), without naming a provider or implying the programme is available in the UK. Give the 30% only as a relative difference in average scores, if at all.
